purpose: Realized Core1 reconstruction chains plus the fresh family instances their practice stages reference, and the cross-core bridge rows checked against them.

operation.name: READ_GIVEN
operation.rule_or_justification: The cubic is x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 and the suggested factor is (x − 1).

derivation.why_valid: Restating the given cubic changes nothing.
derivation.learner_explanation: You are given x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 and asked about (x − 1).

operation.name: SUBSTITUTE
operation.rule_or_justification: Put x = 1 into every term of x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6.

derivation.why_valid: A polynomial accepts every real input, so this substitution is legal.
derivation.learner_explanation: Replace each x in x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 by 1.

equivalence_witness.precondition: x = 1 lies in the domain of the polynomial, so substituting it preserves the value.

operation.name: EVALUATE
operation.rule_or_justification: Work the four terms of x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 out at x = 1.

derivation.why_valid: Each term is evaluated by ordinary arithmetic.
derivation.learner_explanation: The terms come to 1 − 6 + 11 − 6, which is 0, so p(1) = 0 exactly.

operation.name: APPLY_THEOREM
operation.rule_or_justification: p(1) = 0, so by the factor theorem (x − 1) divides the cubic exactly.

derivation.why_valid: The factor theorem turns the value 0 into a divisibility statement.
derivation.learner_explanation: Because p(1) came out as 0, (x − 1) really is a factor of x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6.

operation.name: DIVIDE
operation.rule_or_justification: Divide x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 by (x − 1); the division is exact and leaves (x² − 5x + 6).

derivation.why_valid: The remainder is p(1) = 0, so the quotient is a quadratic.
derivation.learner_explanation: Dividing x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 by (x − 1) leaves (x² − 5x + 6) with nothing over.

equivalence_witness.precondition: The division is exact because p(1) = 0, so no remainder term is dropped.

operation.name: FACTOR
operation.rule_or_justification: Factorise (x² − 5x + 6) by finding two numbers with sum 5 and product 6.

derivation.why_valid: Two numbers with the required sum and product give the linear factors directly.
derivation.learner_explanation: (x² − 5x + 6) splits using 2 and 3, so x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 is now fully factorised.

equivalence_witness.precondition: (x² − 5x + 6) factorises over the integers, so the split loses no solutions.

operation.name: CHECK
operation.rule_or_justification: Multiply the three factors back out and expect x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 term for term.

derivation.why_valid: A factorisation is only correct if expanding returns the original polynomial.
derivation.learner_explanation: Expanding the three factors returns x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6, so the factorisation is right.

H1.text: A suggested factor (x − 1) points at one value of x. Which value, and what must p do there?

H2.text: Test that value in x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 rather than dividing first.

H3.text: Substitute into every term of x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 and evaluate the numbers before deciding anything.

independent_verification.statement: Multiply the three factors out. The expansion must return x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 term for term, with no leftover terms.

answer_custody.quick_check: Do the three factors multiply to give a cubic?

forward.condition: p(a) = 0 for a polynomial p and a number a
forward.conclusion: (x − a) is a factor of p(x)

converse.condition: (x − a) is a factor of p(x)
converse.conclusion: p(a) = 0 for a polynomial p and a number a
converse.justification: If (x − a) divides p(x) exactly then p(x) = (x − a)q(x), and putting x = a gives p(a) = 0.

stages.learner_heading: Start with something you can see
stages.prose: A cubic can sometimes be split into three simple brackets. Before dividing anything, it is worth asking whether one particular bracket works at all, because testing is much quicker than dividing.
Think of p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + R as a division sum written sideways: the bracket is the divisor, q(x) is the quotient and R is whatever is left over.

Dividing by a bracket of the form (x − a) can only leave a plain number behind, never another x term, because the remainder has to be of lower degree than the divisor. That single fact is what makes the whole test work, and it is worth being sure of it before going on.

operation.name: WRITE_DIVISION_FORM
operation.rule_or_justification: Any polynomial divided by (x − a) leaves a quotient and a constant remainder R.

derivation.why_valid: Division by a linear polynomial always leaves a remainder of degree 0.
derivation.learner_explanation: Write p(x) as (x − a)q(x) + R, where R is just a number.

operation.name: SUBSTITUTE
operation.rule_or_justification: Put x = a into p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + R.

derivation.why_valid: The identity holds for every x, so it holds at x = a.
derivation.learner_explanation: At x = a the bracket (a − a) is 0, whatever q(a) happens to be.

equivalence_witness.precondition: The division identity holds for every real x, so x = a is an admissible choice.

operation.name: SIMPLIFY
operation.rule_or_justification: (a − a) is 0, so the whole first product vanishes.

derivation.why_valid: Zero times any number is zero, so only R survives.
derivation.learner_explanation: That leaves p(a) = R, so the remainder is exactly the value of p at a.

operation.name: APPLY_THEOREM
operation.rule_or_justification: (x − a) is a factor precisely when the remainder R is 0, and R = p(a).

derivation.why_valid: Being a factor means the remainder is zero, and the remainder has just been identified as p(a).
derivation.learner_explanation: So testing p(a) is the same as testing whether (x − a) divides p(x).

stages.prose: Expand your three brackets and compare every term with the cubic you started from. If one term differs, the factorisation is wrong even if the test value came out as zero.

forward.condition: a and b are both rational numbers

converse.conclusion: a and b are both rational numbers
converse.justification: A rational product does not force either factor to be rational.

theorem_direction.counterexample_when_converse_false: √2 × √2 = 2 is rational while neither factor is.

stages.learner_heading: Start with something you can see
stages.prose: It is tempting to assume that multiplying two numbers with endless decimals must give another number with endless decimals.

operation.name: IDENTIFY_STRUCTURE
operation.rule_or_justification: The statement is a universal claim: it says something about every pair of irrational numbers.

derivation.why_valid: Naming the shape of the claim does not change it.
derivation.learner_explanation: A claim about every pair can be destroyed by a single pair.

operation.name: WRITE_AS_IMPLICATION
operation.rule_or_justification: Write the claim as a condition and a conclusion so the counterexample has something definite to break.

derivation.why_valid: An implication is false exactly when the condition holds and the conclusion fails.
derivation.learner_explanation: So look for two irrational numbers whose product is rational.

operation.name: SUBSTITUTE
operation.rule_or_justification: Try the most obvious edge case: take a and b to be the same irrational number √2.

derivation.why_valid: √2 is irrational, so it is an admissible choice for both a and b.
derivation.learner_explanation: √2 × √2 is 2, and 2 is a whole number, so the product is rational.

equivalence_witness.precondition: √2 is a real irrational number, so choosing it for both factors is a legal instance of the claim.

operation.name: APPLY_THEOREM
operation.rule_or_justification: The condition held and the conclusion failed, so the universal claim is false.

derivation.why_valid: One counterexample is enough to refute a universal claim.
derivation.learner_explanation: The pair √2 and √2 satisfies the condition but gives the rational product 2, so the claim cannot be true for every pair.

stages.prose: When a claim says every, one well-chosen pair settles it. Check that your pair really does satisfy the condition before trusting it.

bridge_rows.verification_witness: Evaluate p at the tested value and require exactly 0.
Expand the factors and recover the original cubic term for term.
Check the chosen pair really satisfies the condition of the claim before accepting it as a counterexample.
